## File: `SKILL.md`

### Review: Monitoring

Assesses the parts of monitoring that are visible in infrastructure-as-code and monitoring config: alert rules,
notification routing, dashboards, external probes, diagnostic routing and platform-health alerts. It uses local,
pinned summaries of the Azure Well-Architected Framework and Google's SRE books. Health check endpoints and SLO/SLI
documentation are reviewed by `review-observability`.

This subject is entirely IaC-driven: when `compliance-inventory` reports `iacFound: false`, the orchestrator marks it
`applicable: false` and skips the worker call rather than invoking this skill.

#### Inputs

Monitoring-as-code (alert rules, notification targets, dashboards, probes, SLO definitions), diagnostic or log-export
settings, and telemetry-store IaC, per `compliance-inventory`.

#### Standards (local, authoritative)

- `references/standards/azure-well-architected-monitoring.md` — WAFM-01…WAFM-44 (WAFM-31, WAFM-34, WAFM-44 retired). Always load.
- `references/standards/google-sre-monitoring-alerting.md` — SREM-01…SREM-28. Always load.
- Do **not** fetch any URL for this skill. Do not load `references/standards/MAINTENANCE.md`.
- If no element covers a situation: apply the closest element if it clearly fits; otherwise mark the check N/A
  ("not covered by localized standard") and add `localized-standard-gap: <description>` to `notes`.

#### Procedure

1. Load `references/checklist.md`, `references/sources.md`, `references/monitoring-iac-signals.md` and the two
   standards files.
2. Classify each file against `monitoring-iac-signals.md` (alert rule, notification target, dashboard, probe,
   diagnostic routing, platform-health alert, SLO definition, telemetry store). Every active element is generic and
   applies to any cloud, Kubernetes or SaaS monitoring stack; retired rows are not evaluated.
3. No monitoring-as-code: if no file defines an alert rule or a dashboard, fail MON-02 (confidence `high`) and MON-01
   (confidence `low`; note that alerting configured only in a portal can't be seen from the repo), mark MON-03,
   MON-04 and MON-05 N/A ("no monitoring-as-code in scope"), and still evaluate MON-06.
4. Stated SLO: find any SLO, SLI target or availability target in the files (docs, IaC SLO resources, SLO recording
   rules, tags, alert descriptions). If none is stated, skip SLO-dependent elements (SREM-13, the target part of
   WAFM-27, the SLO-derived part of WAFM-14) with reason "no stated SLO to judge against". Never fail for the missing
   SLO itself (that is OBS-07).
5. For each check (MON-01…MON-06), evaluate only the elements it lists whose "Applies when" condition holds. If none
   apply, mark the check N/A with that reason. Security-event alerting (WAFM-41/42 under MON-01, WAFM-43/44 under
   MON-04) applies only when the IaC defines the resources whose signals it alerts on; fail it only when such resources
   exist and no alert rule or SIEM routing covers them (confidence `medium`; portal-configured SIEM rules can't be seen).
6. Retention (WAFM-36, SREM-26): fail only when retention is missing or below a stated requirement. Never fail for
   keeping more (telemetry cost is assessed by `review-cost-sustainability`).
7. Evidence rule: fail only on concrete evidence in the files, e.g. a single-sample evaluation window, an alert rule
   with no notification target, a dashboard with only CPU panels, a resource with no diagnostic routing. Don't fail
   for a missing health endpoint (OBS-06) or for code-level instrumentation (`review-observability`). Use confidence
   `medium` unless the evidence is unambiguous.
8. Severity: every Finding takes the check's default severity from `checklist.md` regardless of element level;
   `checkResults.severityIfFailed` is always that default.
9. Citations: set `element` to the failed element's ID (e.g. `WAFM-01`); the report script derives `standard` and
   `url` from it, so don't write them.
10. Boundaries: **owned here** — all alert rules (MON-01/03), including latency-percentile, retry/failure-rate,
    dead-letter and security-event alerts (sign-in failure spikes, privileged changes, secret-access anomalies,
    WAF/firewall blocks) and their routing to a security owner or SIEM (MON-04); dashboards (MON-05); external probes
    and their thresholds (MON-06, WAFM-32); retention (step 6); telemetry-store access control (WAFM-37); alert-rule
    tests (SREM-08, MON-02). **Don't fail for** code instrumentation, health-endpoint implementation or SLO
    documentation (review-observability; see step 7); load-balancer routing and restart probe configuration
    (review-reliability AZRL-49/50; MON-06 judges only probes that raise alerts, WAFM-32); backup success and
    failover readiness as recovery posture (review-disaster-recovery; this skill judges only the alert rules);
    telemetry cost, sampling and over-retention (review-cost-sustainability; see step 6); sensitive data or secrets
    in log content (review-security-operational); application unit and integration tests (review-testing; alert-rule
    tests stay here).

#### Output

Findings, strengths and check results per `compliance-review-core`'s `finding-schema.md`.

This checklist keeps only the checks that need infrastructure-as-code or monitoring config to evaluate; the subject is skipped entirely (N/A) when `iacFound` is false — see `compliance-inventory`.

## File: `references/monitoring-iac-signals.md`

### Monitoring-as-code signals

Local lookup table, not a standard. Use it to classify each file in the subject's list (`SKILL.md` step 2). Only the
resource types and files below count as monitoring-as-code. If a monitoring resource type isn't listed, apply the
closest row only when it clearly fits; otherwise add `localized-standard-gap: unrecognized monitoring resource <type>`
to `notes`.

"Alert rule" and "Dashboard" are the two signals that decide the no-monitoring-as-code rule (`SKILL.md` step 3).

#### Resource types per platform

| Signal | Azure (Bicep / ARM / Terraform `azurerm`) | AWS (CloudFormation / Terraform `aws`) | GCP (Terraform `google`) | Kubernetes / Prometheus / Grafana | Datadog (Terraform `datadog`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alert rule | `Microsoft.Insights/metricAlerts`, `Microsoft.Insights/scheduledQueryRules`, `Microsoft.Insights/activityLogAlerts`, `Microsoft.AlertsManagement/prometheusRuleGroups`; `azurerm_monitor_metric_alert`, `azurerm_monitor_scheduled_query_rules_alert_v2`, `azurerm_monitor_activity_log_alert`, `azurerm_monitor_alert_prometheus_rule_group` | `AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm`, `AWS::CloudWatch::CompositeAlarm`; `aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm`, `aws_cloudwatch_composite_alarm`, `aws_prometheus_rule_group_namespace` | `google_monitoring_alert_policy` | `PrometheusRule` (prometheus-operator CRD); Prometheus rule files (`groups:` with `alert:` entries, often `*.rules.yml`, `*rules*.yaml`); `grafana_rule_group` | `datadog_monitor` |
| Notification target / routing | `Microsoft.Insights/actionGroups`, `Microsoft.AlertsManagement/actionRules` (alert processing rules); `azurerm_monitor_action_group`, `azurerm_monitor_alert_processing_rule_*` | `AWS::SNS::Topic` / `AWS::SNS::Subscription` used as alarm actions; `aws_sns_topic`, `aws_sns_topic_subscription`, `aws_prometheus_alert_manager_definition` | `google_monitoring_notification_channel` | `alertmanager.yml` / `alertmanager*.yaml` (`route`, `receivers`, `inhibit_rules`), `AlertmanagerConfig` CRD; `grafana_contact_point`, `grafana_notification_policy` | `@` notify handles in `datadog_monitor` messages |
| Dashboard | `Microsoft.Portal/dashboards`, `Microsoft.Insights/workbooks`, `Microsoft.Dashboard/grafana`; `azurerm_portal_dashboard`, `azurerm_application_insights_workbook`, `azurerm_dashboard_grafana` | `AWS::CloudWatch::Dashboard`; `aws_cloudwatch_dashboard` | `google_monitoring_dashboard` | Grafana dashboard JSON (`"panels"` + `"title"`), `grafana_dashboard`, `GrafanaDashboard` (grafana-operator CRD), ConfigMaps labelled for the Grafana dashboard sidecar | `datadog_dashboard`, `datadog_dashboard_json` |
| Probe / availability test | `Microsoft.Insights/webtests`; `azurerm_application_insights_standard_web_test`; Network Watcher connection monitors | `AWS::Synthetics::Canary`, `AWS::Route53::HealthCheck`; `aws_synthetics_canary`, `aws_route53_health_check` | `google_monitoring_uptime_check_config` | `Probe` (prometheus-operator CRD) / blackbox-exporter config | `datadog_synthetics_test` |
| Diagnostic routing | `Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings`; `azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting`; Azure Policy assignments with `deployIfNotExists` for diagnostic settings | CloudWatch Logs subscription filters, `aws_flow_log`, `aws_cloudtrail`; container/agent log configuration | `google_logging_project_sink` (and folder/org sinks) | `ServiceMonitor` / `PodMonitor` CRDs, scrape configs, OpenTelemetry Collector / agent config | Datadog agent / integration config |
| Platform-health alert | `activityLogAlerts` with category `ServiceHealth` or `ResourceHealth` | EventBridge rule (`AWS::Events::Rule`, `aws_cloudwatch_event_rule`) with `source: aws.health` | Alert policy on Personalized Service Health events | — | — |
| SLO definition | Stated in docs, tags or alert-rule descriptions | `AWS::ApplicationSignals::ServiceLevelObjective` | `google_monitoring_slo` | OpenSLO or Sloth specs (`PrometheusServiceLevel`), SLO recording rules | `datadog_service_level_objective` |
| Telemetry store | `Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces` (`retentionInDays`), `Microsoft.Insights/components`, `Microsoft.Monitor/accounts`; `azurerm_log_analytics_workspace`, `azurerm_application_insights`; resource locks on these | `aws_cloudwatch_log_group` (`retention_in_days`), `aws_prometheus_workspace` | `google_logging_project_bucket_config` (`retention_days`) | Prometheus / Loki / Tempo / Mimir retention settings, persistent volumes for them | — |

#### Other files that count

- CI steps that validate monitoring config (e.g. `promtool check rules`, `promtool test rules`, `amtool check-config`, rule unit-test files): MON-02 evidence (SREM-08).
- Self-hosted monitoring stack manifests or Helm values (Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, Loki, OpenTelemetry Collector): MON-06 evidence (WAFM-38, SREM-27, SREM-28).

## File: `references/standards/azure-well-architected-monitoring.md`

*Load rule: WAFM-01…WAFM-44 (WAFM-31, WAFM-34, WAFM-44 retired). Always load.*

### Azure Well-Architected Framework — Monitoring and alerting — localized summary

- Level: every element is `REVIEW` (the source uses no normative keywords); severity is the owning check's default.
- Scope column: G = generic (any cloud / Kubernetes / SaaS monitoring). Every active element is Scope G. The Azure-only elements were retired on 2026-11-12; each had a G counterpart that still applies to Azure IaC.

`oe-check` (OE:07) and `re-check` (RE:10) are traceability only: OE:07 = "design a monitoring stack that captures operational telemetry, metrics and logs"; RE:10 = "continuously measure and track system health … retained and accessible".

#### MON-01 — Alert coverage of key failure conditions

| ID | Level | Scope | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WAFM-01 | REVIEW | G | Alert rules cover failed requests / error rate for each user-facing service or entry point. | user-facing service in IaC |
| WAFM-02 | REVIEW | G | Alert rules cover latency on user-facing flows, using percentiles (p95/p99) rather than averages. | user-facing service |
| WAFM-03 | REVIEW | G | Alert rules cover resource exhaustion and capacity limits (CPU, memory, disk, connections, quotas) of constrained resources, and the capacity ceiling of each deployment unit or stamp. | compute/data resources in IaC |
| WAFM-04 | REVIEW | G | Alerts exist at two levels: end-to-end user experience and critical internal transactions, not only resource metrics. | user-facing service |
| WAFM-05 | REVIEW | G | Asynchronous flows are covered on completion as well as acceptance (queue depth or oldest-message age). | queues/event streams in IaC |
| WAFM-06 | REVIEW | G | Critical scheduled or background jobs are monitored for both execution and a valid result (ran on schedule; output not empty or malformed). | scheduled jobs in IaC |
| WAFM-07 | REVIEW | G | Dependency health is covered: dependency error rate, timeouts and latency, or indirect signals when the dependency can't be alerted on directly; retry and transient-fault rates. | external/backend dependencies |
| WAFM-08 | REVIEW | G | The data/storage layer is covered: availability, write failures, query latency, timeouts, locks and resource pressure. | data stores in IaC |
| WAFM-09 | REVIEW | G | Where several instances, zones or regions are deployed, load imbalance across them and standby-region readiness are monitored. | redundant instances/regions |
| WAFM-10 | REVIEW | G | Scaling behaviour is observable: scale-out/scale-in events and cold-start latency. | autoscaling in IaC |
| WAFM-41 | REVIEW | G | Alert rules cover identity and access security signals the IaC can express: sign-in or authorization failure spikes against a baseline, privilege escalation and role or policy changes, account creation or deletion, and unusual secret or key access. | identity, secret-store or role resources, or auth logs routed, in IaC |
| WAFM-42 | REVIEW | G | Alert rules cover unexpected system and network security events: resource creation or deletion and configuration drift, failed patch or update runs, and firewall/WAF denies or unexpected DNS destinations. | firewall, WAF, network or update-management resources in IaC |

#### MON-02 — Alerts and dashboards are defined as code

| ID | Level | Scope | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WAFM-11 | REVIEW | G | Alert rules, notification targets, dashboards and health definitions are version-controlled IaC or config, not only portal-built. | always (IaC present) |
| WAFM-12 | REVIEW | G | Monitoring config is deployed by automation with the workload, so it stays current as components are added or removed. | monitoring-as-code present |
| WAFM-13 | REVIEW | G | Monitoring and alerting are included in workload testing (rules are validated, not only deployed). | monitoring-as-code present |

#### MON-03 — Alert quality and actionability

| ID | Level | Scope | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WAFM-14 | REVIEW | G | Thresholds reflect workload health: derived from SLOs (when stated) or historical baselines, not arbitrary values, and fit load that varies by time of day or season. | alert rules present |
| WAFM-15 | REVIEW | G | Alerts trigger on a sustained breach over an evaluation window, not on a single sample or transient blip. | alert rules present |
| WAFM-16 | REVIEW | G | Each alert carries context: condition and threshold breached, likely impact, components involved, where to investigate. | alert rules present |
| WAFM-17 | REVIEW | G | Alerts are classified by severity (e.g. critical, warning, informational), aligned with customer impact. | alert rules present |
| WAFM-18 | REVIEW | G | Correlated signals are aggregated (health state, composite or grouped alert) so one failure raises one alert, not a per-resource alert storm. | several alert rules on related resources |
| WAFM-19 | REVIEW | G | Alerts are scoped deliberately; production alerting is driven by production data, not mixed with non-production signals. | alert rules + multiple environments |

#### MON-04 — Alert routing and ownership

| ID | Level | Scope | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WAFM-20 | REVIEW | G | Every alert rule is wired to a notification target (action group, receiver, topic, channel). No orphaned rules. | alert rules present |
| WAFM-21 | REVIEW | G | Each alert has an owning team; business-flow alerts reach application owners and component alerts reach operators. | alert rules present |
| WAFM-22 | REVIEW | G | Alerts integrate with incident/ticketing tooling and, where safe, automated remediation or scaling, and tie into operational runbooks. | alert rules present |
| WAFM-43 | REVIEW | G | Security alerts and security-relevant logs are routed to a security owner or a SIEM where they are correlated across sources, not only to the operations channel, and the security data sink outlives the resources it watches. | security alert rules or security logs in IaC |

#### MON-05 — Dashboards present actionable health

| ID | Level | Scope | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WAFM-23 | REVIEW | G | Dashboards are organized around health (healthy / degraded / unhealthy), with drill-down from workload to component. | dashboards present |
| WAFM-24 | REVIEW | G | Dashboards show actionable signals (availability, latency, errors, saturation) and business KPIs with supporting technical indicators, without decorative or redundant panels. | dashboards present |
| WAFM-25 | REVIEW | G | Dashboards are tailored to their audience and use (developers, operators, business stakeholders). | dashboards present |
| WAFM-26 | REVIEW | G | Dashboards are parameterized for exploration (time range, environment, service, region or deployment). | dashboards present |
| WAFM-27 | REVIEW | G | Target attainment (SLO/SLA, when stated) and longer-term trends (weekly/monthly) are visualized, not only real-time state. | dashboards present |
| WAFM-28 | REVIEW | G | Health states are shown with text labels as well as colour (accessibility). | health dashboards present |
| WAFM-29 | REVIEW | G | Operator dashboards and status APIs that drive decisions are themselves monitored for stale or wrong values. | admin dashboards/status APIs in scope |

#### MON-06 — Telemetry reaches monitoring from all layers

| ID | Level | Scope | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WAFM-30 | REVIEW | G | Every deployed resource routes its platform metrics and resource logs to the chosen monitoring backend (diagnostic settings, log export, agents). | IaC resources |
| WAFM-32 | REVIEW | G | External (black-box) probes or availability tests check user-facing endpoints or health endpoints and feed alerts. | user-facing endpoint |
| WAFM-33 | REVIEW | G | Cloud-provider health events (outages, planned maintenance, advisories) notify the team. | cloud IaC |
| WAFM-35 | REVIEW | G | The network layer is monitored where network IaC exists: connectivity/latency checks, flow logs. | network IaC |
| WAFM-36 | REVIEW | G | Telemetry retention is set explicitly to meet operational and stated compliance needs, so incident data isn't deleted too early. Sufficiency only: never fail for keeping more. | telemetry store in IaC |
| WAFM-37 | REVIEW | G | Telemetry stores are protected like production data: access control, soft delete or resource locks against accidental change or deletion. | telemetry store in IaC |
| WAFM-38 | REVIEW | G | Self-managed telemetry pipelines buffer or queue ingestion and are redundant, so spikes don't lose data. | custom telemetry pipeline in IaC |
| WAFM-39 | REVIEW | G | Multi-region workloads collect telemetry regionally and aggregate centrally; business-critical workloads keep autonomous (per-region) telemetry storage. | multi-region IaC |
| WAFM-40 | REVIEW | G | Production telemetry is stored separately from non-production telemetry. | multiple environments in IaC |

## File: `references/standards/google-sre-monitoring-alerting.md`

*Load rule: SREM-01…SREM-28. Always load.*

### Google SRE — Monitoring and alerting — localized summary

- Licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Rows are summaries in our own words; no tables or passages are copied.
- Level: `SHOULD` where the summarized sentence says "should" or "(strongly) recommend/advise", otherwise `REVIEW`. The level never changes severity; severity is the owning check's default.

#### MON-01 — Alert coverage of key failure conditions

| ID | Level | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|
| SREM-01 | REVIEW | User-facing services are alerted on the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (saturation when *nearly* problematic). | user-facing service |
| SREM-02 | REVIEW | Errors include implicit failures (wrong content) and policy failures (too slow); latency of failed requests is tracked separately from successful ones. | user-facing service |
| SREM-03 | REVIEW | Resources with hard limits, or whose use degrades performance past a threshold, have approaching-exhaustion alerts, including predictive ones (e.g. disk full in N hours). | compute/data resources |
| SREM-04 | REVIEW | Sudden, severe changes in user request rate are detected by a simple rule. | user-facing service |
| SREM-05 | SHOULD | Responses from direct dependencies are monitored (latency, response codes, sizes), ideally once in the shared client library. | dependencies |

#### MON-02 — Alerts and dashboards are defined as code

| ID | Level | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|
| SREM-06 | SHOULD | Monitoring configuration is code in version control with review; intent-based config is preferred over UI- or CRUD-only setup. | always (IaC present) |
| SREM-07 | REVIEW | Rules are templated and reused across targets instead of copy-pasted, and every service gets a consistent baseline of metrics and dashboards. | monitoring-as-code present |
| SREM-08 | SHOULD | Alerting logic is tested: config linting, rule unit tests with synthetic series (e.g. `promtool test rules`) and routing tests, preferably in CI. | monitoring-as-code present |
| SREM-09 | SHOULD | Alerting parameters (windows, burn rates) are shared across services or request-class buckets, not hand-tuned per service. | several services alerted |

#### MON-03 — Alert quality and actionability

| ID | Level | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|
| SREM-10 | REVIEW | Paging alerts target symptoms (user-visible impact); cause-based alerts are kept for definite, imminent problems. | alert rules present |
| SREM-11 | SHOULD | Every page is urgent and actionable; conditions with a rote, scriptable response are automated rather than paged. | alert rules present |
| SREM-12 | REVIEW | Threshold alerts tolerate flapping with a minimum pending duration (≥ 2 evaluation cycles); SLO alerts use windowed burn rates instead of long durations. | alert rules present |
| SREM-13 | SHOULD | When an SLO is stated, alerts use multiwindow, multi-burn-rate rules. Starting point for 99.9 %: page at 2 % of budget in 1 h (5 m short window) or 5 % in 6 h (30 m); ticket at 10 % in 3 d (6 h). | stated SLO |
| SREM-14 | REVIEW | Alert design balances precision, recall, detection time and reset time; low-traffic services use synthetic traffic, grouping or longer windows instead of paging on single failures. | stated SLO or low-traffic service |
| SREM-15 | REVIEW | Alerting metrics are counters or ratios that move sharply only in problem states; latency uses histograms/percentiles, not means. | alert rules present |
| SREM-16 | REVIEW | Alert notifications carry context (rule, scope, triggering value) and link to a dashboard, runbook or ready-made query. | alert rules present |
| SREM-17 | SHOULD | Paging rules are simple, predictable and represent a clear failure; complex dependency-hierarchy rules are avoided. | alert rules present |

#### MON-04 — Alert routing and ownership

| ID | Level | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|
| SREM-18 | SHOULD | A severity label routes each alert: pages to on-call, subcritical alerts to a ticket queue, the rest to dashboards only. Email-only alerting is avoided. | alert rules present |
| SREM-19 | REVIEW | Routing de-duplicates and groups alerts and inhibits dependent ones (per-node vs global; downstream vs failing dependency), and inhibition ends when the event ends. | alert routing config present |
| SREM-20 | REVIEW | Pages go to an on-call rotation, and one issue doesn't page several teams. | alert routing config present |

#### MON-05 — Dashboards present actionable health

| ID | Level | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|
| SREM-21 | SHOULD | Service dashboards show the four golden signals, with SLI metrics prominent on the landing view. | dashboards present |
| SREM-22 | SHOULD | Dashboards surface production changes (build or config version, deploy time) so they can be correlated with incidents. | dashboards present |
| SREM-23 | REVIEW | Served traffic can be broken down by status code, including quota or rate-limit rejections. | dashboards present |
| SREM-24 | REVIEW | Dashboards use fitting chart types (histograms/heatmaps for latency), a consistent layout across sets, and label-based drill-down. | dashboards present |

#### MON-06 — Telemetry reaches monitoring from all layers

| ID | Level | Requirement (summary) | Applies when |
|---|---|---|---|
| SREM-25 | REVIEW | Black-box probes check user-visible behaviour, including response content, both at the front door and behind the load balancer, to localize failures. | user-facing endpoint |
| SREM-26 | REVIEW | Summary metrics are kept for months, for trend and capacity analysis. Sufficiency only: never fail for keeping more. | telemetry store in IaC |
| SREM-27 | REVIEW | Collection and rule-evaluation intervals keep alerting data fresh (no more than about 4–5 minutes stale) without needless fine resolution. | scrape/evaluation intervals in config |
| SREM-28 | SHOULD | A self-hosted monitoring stack separates collection, storage, alerting and dashboards behind stable interfaces, and is run like a production service. | self-hosted monitoring stack in IaC |
